content.pt:
História de Solapur

Solapur possui uma história notável e é popularmente conhecida como a “Cidade dos Hutatmas”. Um Hutatma é um lutador pela liberdade que perdeu a vida enquanto lutava contra o domínio britânico.

Os quatro Hutatmas de Solapur

Solapur está associada a quatro importantes lutadores pela liberdade que sacrificaram suas vidas durante a luta pela independência da Índia:

  • Shri Mallappa Dhanshetti
  • Shri Kurban Hussain
  • Shri Jagannath Shinde
  • Shri Kisan Sarda

O papel de Solapur no movimento de independência

Solapur ocupa um lugar único na história da Índia porque seus cidadãos desfrutaram de um breve período de liberdade mesmo antes da independência do país. De 9 a 11 de maio de 1930, Solapur permaneceu praticamente livre do controle britânico.

Após a prisão de Mahatma Gandhi em maio de 1930, protestos e manifestações contra o domínio britânico ocorreram em toda a Índia. Grandes manifestações também foram realizadas em Solapur. Muitos cidadãos perderam a vida durante os disparos da polícia, fazendo com que uma multidão enfurecida atacasse as delegacias.

Diante da situação, policiais e outros funcionários deixaram Solapur. Durante três dias, os cidadãos de Solapur experimentaram um período de autogoverno.

A Bandeira Nacional na Prefeitura de Solapur

O Conselho Municipal de Solapur tem a distinção de ser o primeiro conselho municipal da Índia onde a Bandeira Nacional foi hasteada no edifício municipal em 1930.

Inspirados pela Marcha do Sal de Mahatma Gandhi, os lutadores pela liberdade de Solapur decidiram hastear a Bandeira Nacional no edifício do Conselho Municipal. Em 6 de abril de 1930, o importante lutador pela liberdade Shri Annasaheb Bhopatkar, de Pune, hasteou a Bandeira Nacional sobre o edifício municipal.

As autoridades britânicas reagiram fortemente e declararam lei marcial em Solapur. Muitos líderes e cidadãos foram presos sob várias acusações.

Os quatro lutadores pela liberdade

Shri Mallappa Dhanshetti, Shri Kurban Hussain, Shri Jagannath Shinde e Shri Kisan Sarda foram presos em conexão com a morte de dois policiais da delegacia de Mangalwar.

Eles foram condenados à morte e executados em 12 de janeiro de 1931 na prisão de Pune. Seu sacrifício deu a Solapur a identidade permanente de “Cidade dos Hutatmas”.

Como Chegar a Solapur

Por estrada

Solapur está localizada a aproximadamente 410 km de Mumbai e possui boas conexões rodoviárias e ferroviárias. A cidade está situada em importantes rotas que conectam Mumbai ao sul e ao centro da Índia.

  • Pune: aproximadamente 245 km
  • Hyderabad: aproximadamente 305 km
  • Mumbai: aproximadamente 410 km

As rodovias nacionais NH-9, NH-13 e NH-211 passam pela cidade, tornando Solapur um importante centro comercial.

De trem

Solapur possui boas conexões ferroviárias e está localizada em importantes rotas que ligam Mumbai ao sul da Índia e a Hyderabad.

Comida em Solapur

Solapur é um importante destino religioso para pessoas de Maharashtra e de outras partes da Índia. Localizada em uma rota de peregrinação hindu, a cidade recebe muitos peregrinos e turistas que viajam para a vizinha Karnataka.

Por isso, os restaurantes de Solapur oferecem uma grande variedade de comida vegetariana. Muitos restaurantes também possuem nomes associados às tradições religiosas hindus, como Annapurna e Upasana.

Comida tradicional

Durante os festivais hindus, é comum servir comida aos peregrinos nos templos. As refeições tradicionais podem incluir arroz, vegetais e lentilhas, seguidos por uma sobremesa popular de Solapur chamada “Lapshi”. Ela é preparada com trigo quebrado ou sêmola de trigo misturada com açúcar mascavo ou açúcar.

Dhabas locais

Solapur também possui restaurantes locais de estrada conhecidos como Dhabas. Esses estabelecimentos servem refeições preparadas na hora em um ambiente simples e informal.

Um Thali vegetariano tradicional geralmente inclui arroz, pão indiano, lentilhas, vegetais e uma sobremesa. Muitos restaurantes oferecem porções generosas e reposição.

Barracas de comida, cafés e cantinas também podem ser encontrados próximos a centros comerciais, escolas e instituições educacionais.

content.es:
Historia de Thane

A lo largo de su historia, Thane ha sido conocida con diferentes nombres. Se cree que su nombre actual deriva de Sthan o Sthanaka, la capital de los gobernantes Shilahara de Konkan.

Las primeras referencias a Thane aparecen en los escritos del geógrafo griego Ptolomeo, quien entre los años 135 y 150 d.C. mencionó un lugar llamado Quersoneso. Según las investigaciones, esta zona correspondía al área alrededor del arroyo de Thane.

Thane vuelve a aparecer en registros medievales a través de placas de cobre e inscripciones descubiertas en la ciudad. Una de estas placas, descubierta cerca de los cimientos del Fuerte de Thane en 1787 y fechada en 1078 d.C., registra una concesión de tierras de Arikesara Devaraja y menciona una ciudad llamada Sri Sthanaka.

Thane como puerto medieval

El viajero veneciano Marco Polo visitó Thane alrededor de 1290 d.C. y describió la ciudad como un reino próspero con un puerto desarrollado. Mencionó el continuo tráfico de barcos y el comercio de productos como telas, cuero y algodón, además de la importación de caballos.

El fraile Giordano visitó Thane entre 1321 y 1324 y describió la ciudad bajo administración musulmana. También dejó información sobre la presencia cristiana temprana en Thane.

Viajeros como Ibn Battuta y Abul Feda también mencionaron Thane con el nombre de Kukin Tana y destacaron su importancia como puerto. La ciudad estaba asociada con la producción de un tipo de tejido conocido como “Tanasi”.

Dominio portugués y maratha

Los portugueses llegaron a Thane en 1530 y gobernaron la región durante más de 200 años, hasta 1739. Durante este período, Thane era conocida como Cacabe de Tana. La construcción del Fuerte de Thane comenzó en 1730.

Los marathas conquistaron Bassein y Thane en 1737 y 1739. Su dominio continuó hasta 1784, cuando los británicos capturaron el fuerte y establecieron Thane como un importante centro administrativo.

Periodo británico y administración municipal

Bajo el dominio británico, Thane se convirtió en la sede de la administración del distrito, con un District Collector establecido en la ciudad. El Consejo Municipal de Thane se creó en 1863, cuando la ciudad tenía una población aproximada de 9.000 habitantes.

Thane después de la independencia

Después de la independencia de la India, Thane se desarrolló gradualmente y se convirtió en una importante ciudad industrial durante las décadas de 1960 y 1970. Las actividades comerciales, el transporte y la construcción también crecieron considerablemente.

Durante las décadas de 1980 y 1990, Thane experimentó un rápido desarrollo de la construcción y la vivienda. La población aumentó considerablemente y Thane se consolidó como un importante suburbio de Mumbai.

Cómo llegar a Thane

Por avión

Thane se encuentra aproximadamente a 25 km del aeropuerto internacional situado en Mumbai.

En tren

Thane está conectada mediante líneas ferroviarias de vía ancha con Mumbai y Pune.

Por carretera

Las carreteras nacionales y estatales conectan la sede del distrito de Thane con sus diferentes tehsils y pueblos. La Carretera Nacional 8 atraviesa el distrito y Thane también está conectada con las NH-4 y NH-17.

content.en:
History of Thane

Throughout its history, Thane has been known by several different names. Its present name is believed to have originated from Sthan or Sthanaka, the capital of the Shilahara rulers of Konkan.

The earliest evidence of Thane appears in the writings of the Greek geographer Ptolemy, who referred to a place called Chersonesus between 135 and 150 AD. Research suggests that this area was around Thane Creek.

Thane appears again in medieval records through copper plates and inscriptions discovered in the city. One copper plate discovered near the foundations of Thane Fort in 1787, dated to 1078 AD, records a land grant by Arikesara Devaraja and refers to a city called Sri Sthanaka.

Thane as a Medieval Port

The Venetian traveller Marco Polo visited Thane around 1290 AD and described it as a prosperous kingdom with a developed port. He mentioned continuous maritime traffic and trade in products such as cloth, leather and cotton, as well as the import of horses.

Friar Jordanus visited Thane between 1321 and 1324 and described the city as being under Muslim administration. He also recorded information about the early Christian presence in Thane.

Travellers such as Ibn Battuta and Abul Feda also referred to Thane as Kukin Tana and highlighted its importance as a port. The city was associated with the production of a type of cloth known as “Tanasi”.

Portuguese and Maratha Rule

The Portuguese arrived in Thane in 1530 and ruled the region for more than 200 years, until 1739. During this period, Thane was known as Cacabe de Tana. Construction of Thane Fort began in 1730.

The Marathas conquered Bassein and Thane in 1737 and 1739. Their control continued until 1784, when the British captured the fort and established Thane as an important administrative centre.

British Period and Municipal Administration

Under British rule, Thane became the headquarters of the district administration, with a District Collector stationed in the city. The Thane Municipal Council was established in 1863, when the city had a population of around 9,000.

Thane After Independence

After India's independence, Thane developed gradually and became an important industrial city during the 1960s and 1970s. Commercial activities, transportation and construction also expanded significantly.

During the 1980s and 1990s, Thane experienced rapid development in construction and housing. The city's population increased considerably, and Thane emerged as an important suburb of Mumbai.

How to Reach Thane

By Air

Thane is approximately 25 km from the international airport located in Mumbai.

By Train

Thane is connected by broad-gauge railway lines with Mumbai and Pune.

By Road

National and state highways connect Thane district headquarters with its various tehsils and villages. National Highway 8 passes through the district, while Thane is also connected with NH-4 and NH-17.

Viagem a Thekkady: Santuário de Vida Selvagem, Atividades e Compras

O Santuário de Vida Selvagem de Thekkady é uma fascinante reserva de vida selvagem que se estende por 777 quilómetros quadrados e foi declarada Reserva de Tigres em 1978. O santuário está situado em torno do lago artificial de 24 quilómetros quadrados formado pela barragem de Mullaperiyar sobre o rio Periyar. Existem três torres de observação para observar a vida selvagem em Edappalayam, Manakkavala e Thannikudy.

O Templo de Mangladevi, localizado a 12 km, na fronteira norte da reserva, a famosa cidade de plantações de Peermede, que recebeu o nome do santo sufi Mohammed Peer, Munnar, a popular estação de montanha conhecida pela Neelakurinji, uma flor que cobre as colinas com uma tonalidade azul uma vez a cada doze anos, e Anamudi (2.695 m), o pico mais alto do sul da Índia, são lugares que merecem ser visitados.

Atividades em Thekkady

O Departamento Florestal organiza excursões ecológicas através de plantações de especiarias, café e chá, bem como visitas a fábricas de chá e aldeias tribais nas colinas e arredores.

Para desfrutar da experiência da floresta, pode fazer passeios de elefante, cruzeiros de barco no Lago Periyar e trekking em Kurisumala, Pullumedu, Ottakathalamedu, Grampi, Nellikkampetty e Manakkavala.

O riacho Aruvi (16 km), a Ilha de Crusoe (19 km), Manakkavala (10 km), Mullakudy (29 km), Pavarasu (19 km), a Barragem de Periyar (12 km), Thannikudy (38 km) e Peermede (40 km) são locais ideais para piqueniques.

O Programa de Património Tribal proporciona uma visão sobre o modo de vida tradicional das comunidades tribais através de visitas às aldeias tribais, habitações tradicionais, equipamentos de pesca e caça, plantas medicinais indígenas e ao Museu do Património Tribal.

Como Chegar a Thekkady

De avião

Os aeroportos mais próximos são o de Madurai, a aproximadamente 140 km, o de Kochi, a cerca de 185 km, e o de Thiruvananthapuram, a aproximadamente 265 km.

De comboio

A estação ferroviária mais próxima é Kottayam, situada a cerca de 114 km, enquanto a estação ferroviária de Madurai fica aproximadamente a 136 km.

Por estrada

Uma excelente rede rodoviária a partir de Kumily, localizada a cerca de 4 km, liga Thekkady às principais vilas e cidades de Kerala e a outras partes da Índia.

Compras em Thekkady

Fazer compras em Thekkady é divertido, pois encontrará muitos pequenos artigos para comprar para si, para a sua família e para os seus amigos. Thekkady não possui muitas grandes áreas comerciais, mas uma das principais zonas de compras é Kumily, localizada a cerca de 4 quilómetros.

Não precisa de se preocupar muito com o que comprar em Thekkady, pois o local está repleto de pequenos artigos que podem parecer simples, mas que são bonitos à sua maneira.

Fazer compras é realmente divertido em Thekkady. Poderá sentir-se tentado a comprar quase tudo o que é apresentado nas pequenas e coloridas bancas dos mercados.

Por estar situada no coração da região produtora de especiarias, encontrará alguns dos melhores produtos, como feno-grego, pimenta branca e verde, canela, cardamomo, noz-moscada, anis-estrelado, coentros, cravinho e praticamente todas as especiarias que possa imaginar.

Pode comprar amostras de todas estas especiarias, normalmente embaladas em pequenos sacos transparentes e organizados, com etiquetas impressas.

Saboreie chips de banana acabados de fritar em aromático óleo de coco enquanto percorre os corredores dos mercados de especiarias.

Por fim, não se esqueça de comprar T-shirts de boa qualidade para as crianças, com motivos de tigres e elefantes, como lembrança da sua visita a Kerala.

Travel to Thekkady: Wildlife Sanctuary, Activities and Shopping

Thekkady Wildlife Sanctuary is a fascinating wildlife reserve spread across 777 square kilometres and was declared a Tiger Reserve in 1978. The sanctuary is centred around the 24-square-kilometre artificial lake formed by the Mullaperiyar Dam across the Periyar River. There are three watchtowers for observing wildlife at Edappalayam, Manakkavala and Thannikudy.

The Mangladevi Temple, located 12 km away on the northern boundary of the reserve, the famous plantation town of Peermede, named after the Sufi saint Mohammed Peer, Munnar, the popular hill station known for Neelakurinji, a flower that covers the hills in a blue hue once every twelve years, and Anamudi (2,695 m), the highest peak in South India, are all worth visiting.

Activities in Thekkady

The Forest Department organises eco-tours through spice, coffee and tea plantations, as well as visits to tea factories and tribal villages in and around the hills.

To enjoy the forest experience, you can go on elephant rides, take boat cruises on Periyar Lake and enjoy trekking at Kurisumala, Pullumedu, Ottakathalamedu, Grampi, Nellikkampetty and Manakkavala.

Aruvi stream (16 km), Crusoe Island (19 km), Manakkavala (10 km), Mullakudy (29 km), Pavarasu (19 km), Periyar Dam (12 km), Thannikudy (38 km) and Peermede (40 km) are ideal picnic spots.

The Tribal Heritage Programme provides an insight into the traditional tribal way of life through visits to tribal villages, traditional homes, fishing and hunting equipment, indigenous medicinal plants and the Tribal Heritage Museum.

How to Reach Thekkady

By Air

The nearest airports are Madurai, approximately 140 km away, Kochi, approximately 185 km away, and Thiruvananthapuram, approximately 265 km away.

By Train

The nearest railway station is Kottayam, about 114 km away, while Madurai railway station is approximately 136 km away.

By Road

An excellent road network from Kumily, located about 4 km away, connects Thekkady with all the major towns and cities in Kerala and other parts of India.

Shopping in Thekkady

Shopping in Thekkady is fun, as you will find many small things to buy for yourself, your family and your friends. Thekkady does not have many large shopping areas, but one important shopping area is Kumily, located about 4 kilometres away.

You do not need to worry much about what to buy in Thekkady, as the area is filled with small items that may seem simple but are beautiful in their own way.

Shopping is truly entertaining in Thekkady. You may be tempted to buy almost everything displayed at the small and colourful market stalls.

Being located in the heart of the spice-growing region, you will find some of the finest fenugreek, white and green pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, nutmeg, star anise, coriander, cloves and almost every spice you can imagine.

You can buy samples of all these spices, usually packed neatly in small transparent bags with printed labels.

Enjoy freshly fried banana chips cooked in aromatic coconut oil as you make your way through the maze of spice-market lanes.

Finally, do not forget to buy good-quality T-shirts for children featuring tiger and elephant motifs as a memorable souvenir of your Kerala visit.

Viaje a Thekkady: Santuario de Vida Silvestre, Actividades y Compras

El Santuario de Vida Silvestre de Thekkady es una fascinante reserva de vida silvestre que se extiende por 777 kilómetros cuadrados y que fue declarada Reserva de Tigres en 1978. El santuario se centra alrededor del lago artificial de 24 kilómetros cuadrados formado por la presa de Mullaperiyar sobre el río Periyar. Hay tres torres de vigilancia para observar la vida silvestre en Edappalayam, Manakkavala y Thannikudy.

El Templo Mangladevi, situado a 12 km en el límite norte de la reserva, la famosa ciudad de plantaciones de Peermede, que lleva el nombre del santo sufí Mohammed Peer, Munnar, la popular estación de montaña conocida por el Neelakurinji, una flor que cubre las colinas de un tono azul cada doce años, y el pico más alto del sur de la India, Anamudi (2.695 m), son lugares que merecen una visita.

Actividades en Thekkady

El Departamento Forestal organiza excursiones ecológicas a través de plantaciones de especias, café y té, así como visitas a fábricas de té y aldeas tribales en las colinas y sus alrededores.

Para disfrutar de una auténtica experiencia en el bosque, puedes realizar paseos en elefante, cruceros en barco por el lago Periyar y trekking en Kurisumala, Pullumedu, Ottakathalamedu, Grampi, Nellikkampetty y Manakkavala.

El arroyo Aruvi (16 km), la isla de Crusoe (19 km), Manakkavala (10 km), Mullakudy (29 km), Pavarasu (19 km), la presa de Periyar (12 km), Thannikudy (38 km) y Peermede (40 km) son lugares ideales para hacer un picnic.

El Programa de Patrimonio Tribal ofrece una visión de la forma de vida de las comunidades tribales, con recorridos por aldeas tribales, viviendas tradicionales, utensilios de pesca y caza, plantas medicinales autóctonas y el Museo del Patrimonio Tribal.

Cómo Llegar a Thekkady

En avión

Los aeropuertos más cercanos son el de Madurai, situado a unos 140 km, el de Kochi, a unos 185 km, y el de Thiruvananthapuram, a unos 265 km.

En tren

La estación de tren más cercana es Kottayam, situada a unos 114 km, mientras que la estación de Madurai se encuentra aproximadamente a 136 km.

Por carretera

Una excelente red de carreteras desde Kumily, situada a unos 4 km, conecta Thekkady con los principales pueblos y ciudades de Kerala y otras partes de la India.

Compras en Thekkady

Hacer compras en Thekkady es divertido, ya que encontrarás muchas pequeñas cosas que puedes comprar para ti, tu familia y tus amigos. Thekkady no cuenta con muchas grandes zonas comerciales, pero una de las principales áreas de compras es Kumily, situada a unos 4 kilómetros.

La pregunta de qué comprar en Thekkady no debería preocuparte demasiado, ya que este lugar está lleno de pequeños artículos que pueden parecer sencillos, pero que son hermosos a su manera.

Ir de compras es realmente entretenido en Thekkady. Puedes sentirte tentado a comprar casi todo lo que aparece en los pequeños y coloridos puestos de los mercados.

Debido a su ubicación en el corazón de la región de las especias, encontrarás una gran variedad de productos como alholva, pimienta blanca y verde, canela, cardamomo, nuez moscada, anís estrellado, cilantro, clavo de olor y prácticamente todas las especias que puedas imaginar.

Puedes comprar una muestra de cada una de ellas, normalmente empaquetadas en pequeñas y ordenadas bolsas transparentes con etiquetas impresas.

Mientras recorres los mercados de especias, disfruta de los chips de plátano recién fritos en aromático aceite de coco.

Por último, no olvides comprar camisetas de buena calidad para los niños, decoradas con motivos de tigres y elefantes, como recuerdo de tu visita a Kerala.

Travel to Thrissur: History, Culture and Shopping

Since ancient times, Thrissur district has played an important role in the political history of South India. The early political history of the district is closely connected with the Cheras of the Sangam Age, who ruled over large parts of Kerala and had their capital at Vanchi. The entire present-day Thrissur district was included in the early Chera Empire.

The district also played an important role in promoting trade relations between Kerala and the outside world during ancient and medieval times.

How to Reach Thrissur

By Air

The nearest airport is Cochin International Airport at Nedumbassery, located approximately 58 km from the city. Another major airport near Thrissur is Kochi Airport. Several public and private airlines connect the region with major cities in Kerala and other parts of India.

By Road

An extensive network of roads connects the city with many important destinations in South India.

By Train

Thrissur has an important railway station in South India. Several major trains connect Thrissur with other places in Kerala and neighbouring cities in South India.

Shopping in Thrissur

Thrissur is an important city in Kerala and is often referred to as the cultural capital of the state. Its rich tradition of arts and handicrafts makes shopping in Thrissur a rewarding experience.

Silk weaving and jewellery making are important traditional crafts of Thrissur. The famous Thrissur silk sarees, made with soft silk threads and vibrant colours, are almost a must-buy for anyone looking to take home a special souvenir from Kerala. The city also has many large jewellery stores.

Other traditional Kerala handicrafts such as coir products, coconut-shell crafts, horn sculptures, wood carvings and bronze works are also available in abundance in Thrissur.

Skilled artisans from the region create beautiful carpets, floor coverings and many other utility items and artistic objects using coir fibres and coconut shells. Horn carving is also an exquisite traditional craft of Kerala. You can choose from these items while shopping in Thrissur.

Finally, do not forget to take home Kathakali masks while shopping in Thrissur as souvenirs of your wonderful Kerala trip.

There are many options for shopping in Thrissur. State government emporiums and private shops are available throughout the city.

You can also shop at roadside stalls set up by local vendors, offering a wide variety of products and good opportunities to find attractive bargains.

Food in Thrissur

Kerala is famous throughout the world for its excellent cuisine prepared in traditional ways.

Visitors to Thrissur can enjoy a wide variety of special cuisines served at hotels and fast-food restaurants across the city. Most hotels provide comfortable and quality services to their guests and offer some of the finest traditional Kerala recipes.

The traditional cuisine of the region includes a wide variety of preparations such as boiled dishes, roasted dishes, seafood, vegetables and Chinese food as well.

Some popular Kerala dishes include:

  • Vegetable Korma
  • Fried Fish
  • Dosa
  • Pakoda
  • Banana Chips
  • Erisseri
  • Bonda
  • Palak Paneer
  • Green Beans with Dry Coconut

Todo el actual distrito de Thrissur formaba parte del antiguo Imperio Chera.

El distrito también desempeñó un papel importante en el desarrollo de las relaciones comerciales entre Kerala y el mundo exterior durante las épocas antigua y medieval.

En avión

El aeropuerto más cercano es el Aeropuerto Internacional de Cochin, en Nedumbassery, situado a unos 58 km de la ciudad. Otro aeropuerto importante cerca de Thrissur es el de Kochi. Varias aerolíneas públicas y privadas conectan la región con las principales ciudades de Kerala y de la India.

Por carretera

Una extensa red de carreteras conecta la ciudad con muchos lugares importantes del sur de la India.

En tren

Thrissur cuenta con una importante estación ferroviaria del sur de la India. Varios trenes importantes conectan Thrissur con otros lugares de Kerala y con ciudades de los estados vecinos del sur de la India.

Compras en Thrissur

Thrissur es una ciudad importante de Kerala y a menudo se la conoce como la capital cultural del estado. Su rica tradición artística y artesanal ofrece excelentes oportunidades para hacer compras en Thrissur.

El tejido de seda y la fabricación de joyas son importantes artesanías tradicionales de Thrissur. Los famosos saris de seda de Thrissur, elaborados con hilos de seda suaves y colores vibrantes, son una compra casi imprescindible para quienes desean llevarse un recuerdo especial de Kerala. La ciudad también cuenta con numerosas grandes tiendas de joyería.

Otras artesanías tradicionales de Kerala, como productos de fibra de coco, artesanías hechas con cáscara de coco, esculturas de cuerno, tallas de madera y trabajos de bronce, también se encuentran en abundancia en Thrissur.

Los hábiles artesanos de la región elaboran fantásticas alfombras, revestimientos para el suelo y muchos otros artículos utilitarios y objetos de arte utilizando fibras y cáscaras de coco. La talla de cuerno es también una tradición artesanal muy apreciada de Kerala. Puedes elegir algunos de estos artículos mientras haces compras en Thrissur.

Por último, no olvides llevarte máscaras de Kathakali mientras haces compras en Thrissur como recuerdo de tu maravilloso viaje por Kerala.

También puedes comprar en los puestos callejeros instalados por vendedores locales, que ofrecen una gran variedad de productos y buenas oportunidades para conseguir precios atractivos.

History of Tuticorin

Tuticorin, also known as Thoothukudi, is a port city in southern India with more than 400 years of recorded history. Despite its long history, much of its historical heritage has gradually been forgotten.

How to Reach Tuticorin

By Air

Tuticorin Airport is located about 10 km from the city and connects Tuticorin with several major cities in India. Taxis can be hired from the airport to reach the city. Another nearby airport is located at Vagaikulam in Tirunelveli district.

By Train

Tuticorin is well connected by broad-gauge railway to major cities such as Tirunelveli, Chennai, Mysore, Bangalore, Madurai and Trivandrum.

By Road

Tuticorin is well connected by national highways with Madurai and Tirunelveli. Public and private bus services connect the city with major cities across the state.

For local transportation, visitors can hire taxis and auto-rickshaws and use other local transport services.

content.en:
Travel to Udaipur: History, Culture and Shopping in the City of Lakes

Udaipur, also known as the City of Lakes, is one of the most romantic and picturesque destinations in India. Founded in 1559 by Maharana Udai Singh II, this jewel of Rajasthan reflects the grandeur of the Sisodia Rajputs and their legacy of courage, pride and tradition. If you are planning a trip to Udaipur, get ready to discover forts, floating palaces, vibrant markets and a fascinating history that remains alive in every corner of the city. Contact us for your tailor-made trip.

History of Udaipur: The Royal City of the Sisodia Rajputs

The history of Udaipur begins with a legend. During a hunting expedition, Maharana Udai Singh II encountered a sage meditating beside a lake in the Aravalli range. The saint advised him to establish a city in that location, giving rise to Udaipur. As a tribute, the Dhuni Mata shrine was built at the same spot.

Before the formal founding of the city, the Nouchouki pond already existed, having been excavated by a gypsy woman in the 15th century. The Maharana expanded this lake and created Lake Pichola, now one of the most iconic places to see in Udaipur.

Over the centuries, Udaipur became the capital of the kingdom of Mewar. Unlike many other kingdoms in India, the rulers of Udaipur never accepted submission to the Mughal Empire. One of the most famous episodes in Udaipur's history was the Battle of Haldighati in 1576, where the brave Maharana Pratap fought against Akbar's forces. His loyal horse Chetak, who saved him despite being wounded, is remembered today with a shrine that you can visit.

Climate of Udaipur

The climate in Udaipur is tropical. Summers can be hot, reaching 38 °C, while winters are mild and pleasant, with temperatures dropping to around 11 °C. The best time to travel to Udaipur is from September to March, when temperatures are cooler and more comfortable for exploring the city.

Tribal Culture in Udaipur

Udaipur is also home to several tribal communities, among which the Bhils are particularly notable. They have been known for their archery skills since the time of the Mahabharata. Although their traditional lifestyle has gradually integrated with the urban environment, they still preserve their beliefs, their own deities such as Nandevro (maize) and Gwali (milk), and celebrate fairs such as Baneshwar, held between January and February.

These tribal communities have also played an important role in history, supporting the Rajputs in their military strategies, especially against Muslim and Maratha attacks.

How to Reach Udaipur

  • By Air: Maharana Pratap Airport (Debock) is located 24 km from the city centre. It has regular flights to cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Jaipur, Jodhpur and Aurangabad.
  • By Train: Udaipur is connected by rail with major cities across India. Trains such as the Chetak Express and Mewar Express provide convenient access from Delhi, Jaipur and Ajmer.
  • By Road: The city has good road connections. You can travel from Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Agra or Jodhpur. It is also possible to hire a private car with driver, ideal for customised routes through Rajasthan.

Shopping in Udaipur: Handicrafts and Tradition

Shopping in Udaipur is an essential part of the travel experience. The city offers a wide range of traditional products that reflect the rich Mewari culture:

  • Miniature paintings in Rajput and Mughal styles.
  • Traditional textiles dyed using the batik technique and featuring Bagru and Sanganeri prints.
  • Handcrafted jewellery such as Kundan and silver jewellery.
  • Wood, ceramic and terracotta handicrafts, including lanterns, puppets, decorative objects and utensils.

Among the best markets in Udaipur are:

  • Hathipole Bazar: ideal for traditional paintings and textiles.
  • Bada Bazar: jewellery, clothing and traditional footwear.
  • Shilpgram: a handicraft complex on the outskirts of the city where you can see and purchase products directly from local artisans.

Do not forget to take home a Rajasthani puppet as a souvenir of your visit.

Udaipur: A Journey into History and Romance

A trip to Udaipur is an immersion into the living history of India, where lakes reflect palaces, hills hide stories of resistance and every street comes alive with colour and tradition. Whether you come for its architecture, royal heritage or vibrant markets, Udaipur will win your heart forever.
content.es:
Viaje a Udaipur: historia, cultura y compras en la ciudad de los lagos

Udaipur, también conocida como la Ciudad de los Lagos, es uno de los destinos más románticos y pintorescos de la India. Fundada en 1559 por el Maharana Udai Singh II, esta joya de Rajasthan refleja la grandeza de los Rajputs Sisodia y su legado de valentía, orgullo y tradición. Si estás planeando un viaje a Udaipur, prepárate para descubrir fortalezas, palacios flotantes, mercados vibrantes y una historia fascinante que sigue viva en cada rincón de la ciudad. Contáctanos para tu viaje a medida.

Historia de Udaipur: la ciudad real de los Rajputs Sisodia

La historia de Udaipur comienza con una leyenda. Durante una expedición de caza, el Maharana Udai Singh II encontró a un sabio meditando junto a un lago en la cordillera de Aravalli. El santo le aconsejó fundar una ciudad en ese lugar, lo que dio origen a Udaipur. Como tributo, se construyó el santuario Dhuni Mata en ese mismo punto.

Antes de la fundación formal, ya existía el estanque Nouchouki, excavado por una mujer gitana en el siglo XV. El maharana amplió esta laguna y creó el Lago Pichola, hoy uno de los lugares más emblemáticos que ver en Udaipur.

A lo largo de los siglos, Udaipur se consolidó como la capital del reino de Mewar. A diferencia de otros reinos de la India, los gobernantes de Udaipur nunca aceptaron someterse al Imperio mogol. Uno de los episodios más famosos de la historia de Udaipur fue la batalla de Haldighati en 1576, donde el valiente Maharana Pratap luchó contra las tropas de Akbar. Su leal caballo Chetak, que lo salvó pese a estar herido, es hoy recordado con un santuario que puedes visitar.

Clima de Udaipur

El clima en Udaipur es tropical. Los veranos pueden ser calurosos, alcanzando los 38 °C, mientras que los inviernos son suaves y agradables, con mínimas de hasta 11 °C. La mejor época para viajar a Udaipur es de septiembre a marzo, cuando las temperaturas son más frescas y agradables para explorar la ciudad.

Cultura tribal en Udaipur

Udaipur también es hogar de diversas tribus, entre las que destacan los Bhils. Estos son conocidos por sus habilidades con el arco desde tiempos del Mahabharata. Aunque su estilo de vida tradicional se ha ido integrando con el entorno urbano, aún conservan creencias, dioses propios como Nandevro (maíz) o Gwali (leche), y celebran ferias como la de Baneshwar, que tiene lugar entre enero y febrero.

Estas comunidades tribales también han desempeñado un papel clave en la historia, apoyando a los Rajputs en sus estrategias militares, especialmente contra los ataques musulmanes y marathas.

Cómo llegar a Udaipur

  • En avión: El aeropuerto Maharana Pratap (Debock) está ubicado a 24 km del centro. Tiene vuelos regulares a ciudades como Delhi, Mumbai, Jaipur, Jodhpur y Aurangabad.
  • En tren: Udaipur está conectada por tren con las principales ciudades de India. Trenes como el Chetak Express o Mewar Express facilitan el acceso desde Delhi, Jaipur o Ajmer.
  • En carretera: La ciudad cuenta con buenas conexiones por carretera. Puedes viajar desde Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Agra o Jodhpur. También es posible contratar un coche con conductor privado, ideal para rutas personalizadas por Rajasthan.

Compras en Udaipur: artesanía y tradición

Hacer compras en Udaipur es parte esencial del viaje. La ciudad ofrece una amplia gama de productos típicos que reflejan la rica cultura mewarí:

  • Pinturas en miniatura al estilo Rajput y mogol.
  • Textiles tradicionales teñidos con la técnica de batik y estampados Bagru y Sanganeri.
  • Joyería artesanal como la Kundan y la de plata.
  • Artesanía en madera, cerámica y terracota, incluyendo linternas, títeres, objetos decorativos y utensilios.

Entre los mejores mercados de Udaipur están:

  • Hathipole Bazar: ideal para pinturas y tejidos tradicionales.
  • Bada Bazar: joyería, ropa y calzado típico.
  • Shilpgram: un complejo artesanal a las afueras de la ciudad, donde puedes ver y comprar directamente a los artesanos locales.

No olvides llevarte una marioneta rajasthani como recuerdo de tu visita.

Udaipur: un viaje a la historia y el romanticismo

Un viaje a Udaipur es una inmersión en la historia viva de la India, donde los lagos reflejan los palacios, las colinas esconden historias de resistencia y cada calle vibra con color y tradición. Ya sea que vengas por su arquitectura, su legado real o sus vibrantes mercados, Udaipur te conquistará para siempre.

content.pt:
Travel to Ujjain: History, Culture and Places of Interest

Historical Perspective of Ujjain

The history of the ancient city of Ujjain is closely intertwined with legend. According to one legend, Shiva, the destroyer of the universe, descended to Mrityulok, the land of mortals, to defeat the demon king Tripura.

Another tradition states that Lord Krishna came to Ujjain to study under the great sage Sandipani Muni, who taught his disciples at the Sandipani Muni Ashram.

Apart from these myths, archaeological excavations at a site approximately 6 km north of the city have revealed pottery and iron objects dating back to the 8th century BC.

The Great Kingdoms

The period between the 6th and 3rd centuries BC witnessed the emergence of several ambitious kingdoms. Four major kingdoms, known as the Mahajanapadas, emerged in northern India: Avanti, Vatsa, Kausala and Magadha.

King Chandra Pradyota Mahasena ruled the kingdom of Avanti, with Ujjain as its capital. During the 4th century BC, the Mauryan ruler Chandragupta I ruled over Avanti.

The Great Ruler Ashoka and Buddhism

In the middle of the 3rd century BC, Ashoka became the governor of Avanti (Ujjain) and Taxila, in present-day Pakistan, at the age of 18 during the reign of his father, Bindusara.

Initially, Ashoka ruled harshly and used ruthless methods to annex neighbouring territories. However, in 257 BC he became a devoted follower of Buddhism.

He laid the foundations of numerous stupas, domed structures built to house Buddhist relics, particularly at Sanchi. He also built stupas in Ujjain, one of the first territories under his rule.

Stone and metal images of the Buddha have also been discovered in the district, confirming the influence of Buddhism in and around Ujjain.

The Golden Age

After Ashoka's death in 232 BC, his vast empire began to decline, making way for Indo-Greek and Scythian rulers.

During the 2nd century BC, several waves of the Sakas entered Madhya Pradesh and established the Kshatrapa line of rulers in Ujjain.

The Kshatrapas of Ujjain traced their lineage to Chastana. Indo-Greek influence extended towards Mathura and Ujjain until the establishment of the Gupta dynasty around AD 320.

Chandragupta Vikramaditya, also known as Chandragupta II, ruled approximately from AD 380 to 415. He defeated Rudradaman, the grandson of Chastana and the last ruler of that line.

Vikramaditya is associated with the beginning of the Vikram Samvat era, which begins 57 years before the Christian era. His famous court at Ujjain was renowned for poets and scholars, including the celebrated poet Kalidasa, author of the immortal play Abhigyan Shakuntalam.

Visitors from Distant Lands

During the 5th and 6th centuries AD, Ujjain was an important part of the Gupta Empire. The prosperous plains of northern India attracted the Huns, feared invaders from Central Asia.

Led by Toramana, they entered India around AD 465 and established a small empire.

In AD 533, Yashodharman of Mandsaur defeated them and forced them to retreat, allowing Indian rule to be restored.

In AD 606, Harshavardhana ascended the throne of Kannauj. His reign lasted approximately 41 years and he is regarded as one of the last great Hindu rulers to control a substantial part of the Indian subcontinent.

During his reign, the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited India to study Buddhism. He travelled extensively through Harsha's territories and left descriptions of Bundelkhand, Maheshwar and Ujjain, describing Ujjain as a city of splendour.

Harshavardhana died in AD 647.

The Rajputs and the Rulers of Malwa

After the Guptas, rival groups ruled the Gangetic plains. From the 7th century onwards, the Rajputs became politically active in the Malwa plateau.

The Paramaras rose to prominence during the 11th century until the Sultans of Mandu captured their last ruler, Siladitya.

Ujjain was invaded and plundered at different times by neighbouring rulers, including the Chalukyas of Gujarat, the Chandelas of Bundelkhand and various Rajput rulers, before facing further invasions from the west.

The Sultans Invade Ujjain

The Malwa plateau faced Muslim invasions from the late 12th century onwards. Iltutmish, the second ruler of the Slave dynasty, captured Malwa in AD 1234 and plundered Ujjain.

In AD 1305, Alauddin Khalji, the powerful ruler of the Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, captured Ujjain.

Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq also attacked central India and brought the region under the Delhi Sultanate in AD 1327.

In AD 1351, Firoz Shah Tughlaq ascended the throne of Delhi and appointed Dilawar Khan Ghuri as the governor of Malwa.

Malwa Ruled by the Khalji Sultans

With the rise of Mahmud Khan, a powerful minister of Malwa, an independent dynasty of the Malwa Khalji Sultans was established in AD 1436.

From then until the emergence of the powerful Mughal Empire, Malwa remained an area of conflict between local Rajput rulers, the Malwa Sultans and the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.

For a short period, Ujjain was ruled by the Afghan Sur dynasty under Shujat Khan and his son Baz Bahadur, who was eventually defeated by Akbar in AD 1562.

Akbar successfully subdued most of the regional rulers and took control of the region. Later, his grandson Aurangzeb contributed financially towards preserving the glory of some of Ujjain's ancient temples.

The Maratha Era

Ujjain experienced another wave of invasions in the 17th century, this time by the powerful Marathas.

With the establishment of Maratha dominance, numerous temples were constructed, including the Sidhhi Hara Temple and Gopal Temple.

In AD 1750, Ujjain came under the control of the Scindias, who later shifted their capital to Gwalior.

Following the reorganisation of states on linguistic grounds, Madhya Bharat, the Central Provinces of India and other territories were merged to form the new state of Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

How to Reach Ujjain

Ujjain is an ancient city in central India, located in the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh. It lies on the eastern bank of the Kshipra River and serves as the administrative centre of Ujjain district and division.

In ancient times, the city was known as Ujjayini and, according to the Mahabharata, Ujjayani was the capital of the kingdom of Avanti.

Places of Interest in Ujjain

Ujjain offers numerous religious, historical and cultural attractions. Every year, thousands of visitors from India and around the world come to explore this ancient city.

  • Mahakal Temple
  • Kaal Bhairav
  • Sandipani Ashram
  • Triveni (Nav Graha / Shani)
  • ISKCON Temple
  • Mangalnath
  • Harsiddhi (Durga Temple)
  • Chintaman Ganesh
  • Gad Kalika

How to Reach Ujjain by Air

The nearest airport to Ujjain is Indore Airport. Regular flights operate from Indore to Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Bhopal and Ahmedabad.

How to Reach Ujjain by Rail

Ujjain has several railway stations, including Ujjain City Junction, Vikram Nagar and Chintaman. Regular trains connect Ujjain with several major cities across India.

How to Reach Ujjain by Road

The major bus stations in Ujjain include Devas Gate and Nana Kheda. Major roads connecting Ujjain with other cities include Agar Road, Indore Road, Dewas Road, Maksi Road and Barnagar Road.

A large number of private buses operate on these routes.

Hotels in Ujjain

  • Fort Amla, Ujjain
  • Heritage Welcome, Ujjain
  • Shipra Residency, Ujjain
content.es:
Viaje a Ujjain: Historia, Cultura y Lugares de Interés

Perspectiva Histórica de Ujjain

La historia de la antigua ciudad de Ujjain se entrelaza con numerosas leyendas. Según una de ellas, Shiva, el destructor del universo, descendió a Mrityulok, la tierra de los mortales, para derrotar al rey demonio Tripura.

Otra tradición cuenta que el dios Krishna llegó a Ujjain para estudiar con el gran sabio Sandipani Muni, quien enseñó a sus discípulos en el Sandipani Muni Ashram.

Más allá de los mitos, las excavaciones arqueológicas realizadas en un lugar situado aproximadamente a 6 km al norte de la ciudad han revelado objetos de cerámica y hierro que datan del siglo VIII a.C.

Los Grandes Reinos

El período comprendido entre los siglos VI y III a.C. fue testigo del surgimiento de varios reinos poderosos. Cuatro grandes reinos, conocidos como Mahajanapadas, se establecieron en el norte de la India: Avanti, Vatsa, Kausala y Magadha.

El rey Chandra Pradyota Mahasena gobernó el reino de Avanti, cuya capital era Ujjain. En el siglo IV a.C., el primer gobernante del Imperio Maurya, Chandragupta I, gobernó sobre Avanti.

El Gran Gobernante Ashoka y el Budismo

A mediados del siglo III a.C., Ashoka se convirtió en gobernador de Avanti (Ujjain) y Taxila, en el actual Pakistán, a la edad de 18 años, durante el reinado de su padre, Bindusara.

Al principio, Ashoka gobernó con dureza y utilizó métodos despiadados para anexar territorios vecinos. Sin embargo, en el año 257 a.C. se convirtió en un ferviente seguidor del budismo.

Sentó las bases de numerosos stupas, estructuras abovedadas destinadas a albergar reliquias budistas, especialmente en Sanchi. También construyó stupas en Ujjain, uno de los primeros territorios que gobernó.

Se cree que Ashoka construyó un gran número de stupas en diferentes partes de su imperio. También se han descubierto estatuas de Buda de piedra y metal en el distrito, lo que confirma la influencia del budismo en Ujjain y sus alrededores.

La Edad de Oro

Tras la muerte de Ashoka en el año 232 a.C., su enorme imperio comenzó a desintegrarse, dando paso a diferentes gobernantes indo-griegos y escitas.

Durante el siglo II a.C., varias oleadas de los Sakas llegaron a Madhya Pradesh y establecieron la línea de los príncipes Kshatrapa en Ujjain.

Los Kshatrapas de Ujjain remontaban su linaje a Chastana, relacionado con el mundo greco-romano. La influencia indo-griega se extendió hasta Mathura y Ujjain hasta el establecimiento de la dinastía Gupta, alrededor del año 320 d.C.

Chandragupta Vikramaditya, también conocido como Chandragupta II, gobernó aproximadamente entre los años 380 y 415 d.C. Derrotó a Rudradaman, descendiente de Chastana y último gobernante de aquella línea.

Vikramaditya es recordado por su relación con la era Vikram Samvat, que comienza 57 años antes de la era cristiana. Su famosa corte de Ujjain destacó por sus poetas y eruditos, entre ellos el célebre poeta Kalidasa, autor de la obra inmortal Abhigyan Shakuntalam.

Kalidasa quedó profundamente impresionado por la belleza de Ujjain, una ciudad que durante esta época se convirtió en un importante centro cultural y literario.

Los Visitantes de Tierras Lejanas

Durante los siglos V y VI d.C., Ujjain fue una parte importante del Imperio Gupta. Las prósperas llanuras del norte de la India atrajeron a los hunos, invasores procedentes de Asia Central.

Liderados por Toramana, los hunos entraron en la India alrededor del año 465 d.C. y establecieron un pequeño imperio.

En el año 533 d.C., Yashodharman de Mandsaur los derrotó y los obligó a retirarse, permitiendo la restauración del dominio indio.

En el año 606 d.C., Harshavardhana ascendió al trono de Kannauj. Su reinado duró aproximadamente 41 años y es considerado uno de los últimos grandes gobernantes hindúes que controlaron una parte importante del subcontinente.

Durante su reinado, el peregrino chino Hiuen Tsang visitó la India para estudiar el budismo. Pasó varios años recorriendo el territorio bajo el dominio de Harsha y dejó descripciones de lugares como Bundelkhand, Maheshwar y Ujjain, describiendo Ujjain como una ciudad de gran esplendor.

Harshavardhana murió en el año 647 d.C.

Los Rajputs y los Gobernantes de Malwa

Después de los Gupta, diferentes grupos rivales gobernaron las llanuras del Ganges. A partir del siglo VII, los Rajputs comenzaron a adquirir importancia política en la meseta de Malwa.

Los Paramaras alcanzaron gran prominencia durante el siglo XI, hasta que los sultanes de Mandu capturaron a su último gobernante, Siladitya.

Ujjain fue invadida y saqueada en diferentes momentos por gobernantes vecinos, incluidos los Chalukyas de Gujarat, los Chandelas de Bundelkhand y varios gobernantes Rajput, antes de sufrir nuevas invasiones procedentes del oeste.

Los Sultanes Invaden Ujjain

La meseta de Malwa fue objeto de invasiones musulmanas desde finales del siglo XII. Altamash, segundo gobernante de la dinastía de los Esclavos, capturó Malwa en 1234 d.C. y saqueó Ujjain.

En 1305, Alauddin Khalji, poderoso gobernante de la dinastía Khalji del Sultanato de Delhi, capturó Ujjain.

Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq también atacó la India central y puso la región bajo el control del Sultanato de Delhi en 1327.

En 1351, Firoz Shah Tughlaq ascendió al trono de Delhi y nombró a Dilawar Khan Ghuri gobernador de Malwa.

Malwa Gobernado por los Sultanes Khalji

Con la llegada al poder de Mahmud Khan, un poderoso ministro de Malwa, se estableció en 1436 una dinastía independiente de los sultanes Khalji de Malwa.

Desde entonces, y hasta la aparición del poderoso Imperio mogol, Malwa fue escenario de continuas disputas entre los gobernantes Rajput locales, los sultanes de Malwa y los gobernantes del Sultanato de Delhi.

Durante un breve período, Ujjain fue gobernada por la dinastía afgana Sur bajo Shujat Khan y su hijo Baz Bahadur, quien finalmente fue derrotado por Akbar en 1562.

Akbar consiguió someter a la mayoría de los gobernantes regionales y tomó el control de la región. Posteriormente, su nieto Aurangzeb contribuyó económicamente a preservar la gloria de algunos de los antiguos templos de Ujjain.

La Era Maratha

Ujjain experimentó nuevas invasiones durante el siglo XVII, esta vez por parte de los Marathas.

Con el establecimiento de la hegemonía Maratha se construyeron numerosos templos, entre ellos el Templo Sidhhi Hara y el Templo Gopal.

En 1750, Ujjain pasó a manos de los Scindias, quienes posteriormente trasladaron su capital a Gwalior.

Como consecuencia de la reorganización de los estados por razones lingüísticas, Madhya Bharat, las antiguas Provincias Centrales de la India y otros territorios se fusionaron para formar el nuevo estado de Madhya Pradesh el 1 de noviembre de 1956.

Cómo Llegar a Ujjain

Ujjain es una antigua ciudad del centro de la India, situada en la región de Malwa de Madhya Pradesh. Se encuentra a orillas del río Kshipra y es el centro administrativo del distrito y la división de Ujjain.

En la antigüedad, la ciudad era conocida como Ujjayini y, según el Mahabharata, Ujjayani fue la capital del reino de Avanti.

Lugares de Interés en Ujjain

Ujjain ofrece numerosos lugares de interés religioso, histórico y cultural. Cada año miles de visitantes de la India y de diferentes partes del mundo llegan a esta antigua ciudad.

Entre los principales lugares de interés se encuentran:

  • Templo Mahakal
  • Kaal Bhairav
  • Sandipani Ashram
  • Triveni (Nav Graha / Shani)
  • Templo ISKCON
  • Mangalnath
  • Harsiddhi (Templo Durga)
  • Chintaman Ganesh
  • Gad Kalika

Cómo llegar a Ujjain por avión

El aeropuerto más cercano a Ujjain es el Aeropuerto de Indore. Hay vuelos regulares desde Indore hacia Mumbai, Calcuta, Delhi, Bhopal y Ahmedabad.

Cómo llegar a Ujjain por ferrocarril

Ujjain cuenta con varias estaciones ferroviarias, entre ellas Ujjain City Junction, Vikram Nagar y Chintaman. Existen trenes regulares que conectan Ujjain con numerosas ciudades importantes de la India.

Cómo llegar a Ujjain por carretera

Las principales estaciones de autobuses de Ujjain incluyen Devas Gate y Nana Kheda. Las principales carreteras que conectan Ujjain con otras ciudades son Agar Road, Indore Road, Dewas Road, Maksi Road y Barnagar Road.

Numerosos autobuses privados circulan regularmente por estas rutas.

Travel to Ujjain: History, Culture and Places of Interest

Historical Perspective of Ujjain

The history of the ancient city of Ujjain is closely intertwined with legend. According to one legend, Shiva, the destroyer of the universe, descended to Mrityulok, the land of mortals, to defeat the demon king Tripura.

Another tradition states that Lord Krishna came to Ujjain to study under the great sage Sandipani Muni, who taught his disciples at the Sandipani Muni Ashram.

Apart from these myths, archaeological excavations at a site approximately 6 km north of the city have revealed pottery and iron objects dating back to the 8th century BC.

The Great Kingdoms

The period between the 6th and 3rd centuries BC witnessed the emergence of several ambitious kingdoms. Four major kingdoms, known as the Mahajanapadas, emerged in northern India: Avanti, Vatsa, Kausala and Magadha.

King Chandra Pradyota Mahasena ruled the kingdom of Avanti, with Ujjain as its capital. During the 4th century BC, the Mauryan ruler Chandragupta I ruled over Avanti.

The Great Ruler Ashoka and Buddhism

In the middle of the 3rd century BC, Ashoka became the governor of Avanti (Ujjain) and Taxila, in present-day Pakistan, at the age of 18 during the reign of his father, Bindusara.

Initially, Ashoka ruled harshly and used ruthless methods to annex neighbouring territories. However, in 257 BC he became a devoted follower of Buddhism.

He laid the foundations of numerous stupas, domed structures built to house Buddhist relics, particularly at Sanchi. He also built stupas in Ujjain, one of the first territories under his rule.

Stone and metal images of the Buddha have also been discovered in the district, confirming the influence of Buddhism in and around Ujjain.

The Golden Age

After Ashoka's death in 232 BC, his vast empire began to decline, making way for Indo-Greek and Scythian rulers.

During the 2nd century BC, several waves of the Sakas entered Madhya Pradesh and established the Kshatrapa line of rulers in Ujjain.

The Kshatrapas of Ujjain traced their lineage to Chastana. Indo-Greek influence extended towards Mathura and Ujjain until the establishment of the Gupta dynasty around AD 320.

Chandragupta Vikramaditya, also known as Chandragupta II, ruled approximately from AD 380 to 415. He defeated Rudradaman, the grandson of Chastana and the last ruler of that line.

Vikramaditya is associated with the beginning of the Vikram Samvat era, which begins 57 years before the Christian era. His famous court at Ujjain was renowned for poets and scholars, including the celebrated poet Kalidasa, author of the immortal play Abhigyan Shakuntalam.

Visitors from Distant Lands

During the 5th and 6th centuries AD, Ujjain was an important part of the Gupta Empire. The prosperous plains of northern India attracted the Huns, feared invaders from Central Asia.

Led by Toramana, they entered India around AD 465 and established a small empire.

In AD 533, Yashodharman of Mandsaur defeated them and forced them to retreat, allowing Indian rule to be restored.

In AD 606, Harshavardhana ascended the throne of Kannauj. His reign lasted approximately 41 years and he is regarded as one of the last great Hindu rulers to control a substantial part of the Indian subcontinent.

During his reign, the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited India to study Buddhism. He travelled extensively through Harsha's territories and left descriptions of Bundelkhand, Maheshwar and Ujjain, describing Ujjain as a city of splendour.

Harshavardhana died in AD 647.

The Rajputs and the Rulers of Malwa

After the Guptas, rival groups ruled the Gangetic plains. From the 7th century onwards, the Rajputs became politically active in the Malwa plateau.

The Paramaras rose to prominence during the 11th century until the Sultans of Mandu captured their last ruler, Siladitya.

Ujjain was invaded and plundered at different times by neighbouring rulers, including the Chalukyas of Gujarat, the Chandelas of Bundelkhand and various Rajput rulers, before facing further invasions from the west.

The Sultans Invade Ujjain

The Malwa plateau faced Muslim invasions from the late 12th century onwards. Iltutmish, the second ruler of the Slave dynasty, captured Malwa in AD 1234 and plundered Ujjain.

In AD 1305, Alauddin Khalji, the powerful ruler of the Khalji dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, captured Ujjain.

Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq also attacked central India and brought the region under the Delhi Sultanate in AD 1327.

In AD 1351, Firoz Shah Tughlaq ascended the throne of Delhi and appointed Dilawar Khan Ghuri as the governor of Malwa.

Malwa Ruled by the Khalji Sultans

With the rise of Mahmud Khan, a powerful minister of Malwa, an independent dynasty of the Malwa Khalji Sultans was established in AD 1436.

From then until the emergence of the powerful Mughal Empire, Malwa remained an area of conflict between local Rajput rulers, the Malwa Sultans and the rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.

For a short period, Ujjain was ruled by the Afghan Sur dynasty under Shujat Khan and his son Baz Bahadur, who was eventually defeated by Akbar in AD 1562.

Akbar successfully subdued most of the regional rulers and took control of the region. Later, his grandson Aurangzeb contributed financially towards preserving the glory of some of Ujjain's ancient temples.

The Maratha Era

Ujjain experienced another wave of invasions in the 17th century, this time by the powerful Marathas.

With the establishment of Maratha dominance, numerous temples were constructed, including the Sidhhi Hara Temple and Gopal Temple.

In AD 1750, Ujjain came under the control of the Scindias, who later shifted their capital to Gwalior.

Following the reorganisation of states on linguistic grounds, Madhya Bharat, the Central Provinces of India and other territories were merged to form the new state of Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956.

How to Reach Ujjain

Ujjain is an ancient city in central India, located in the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh. It lies on the eastern bank of the Kshipra River and serves as the administrative centre of Ujjain district and division.

In ancient times, the city was known as Ujjayini and, according to the Mahabharata, Ujjayani was the capital of the kingdom of Avanti.

Places of Interest in Ujjain

Ujjain offers numerous religious, historical and cultural attractions. Every year, thousands of visitors from India and around the world come to explore this ancient city.

  • Mahakal Temple
  • Kaal Bhairav
  • Sandipani Ashram
  • Triveni (Nav Graha / Shani)
  • ISKCON Temple
  • Mangalnath
  • Harsiddhi (Durga Temple)
  • Chintaman Ganesh

How to Reach Ujjain by Air

The nearest airport to Ujjain is Indore Airport. Regular flights operate from Indore to Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Bhopal and Ahmedabad.

How to Reach Ujjain by Rail

Ujjain has several railway stations, including Ujjain City Junction, Vikram Nagar and Chintaman. Regular trains connect Ujjain with several major cities across India.

How to Reach Ujjain by Road

The major bus stations in Ujjain include Devas Gate and Nana Kheda. Major roads connecting Ujjain with other cities include Agar Road, Indore Road, Dewas Road, Maksi Road and Barnagar Road.

A large number of private buses operate on these routes.

Historia de Varanasi

Varanasi, también conocida como Kashi y Benarés, es una de las ciudades habitadas más antiguas del mundo y ha sido un importante destino de peregrinación para los hindúes durante siglos. Según la tradición hindú, Varanasi está asociada con el dios Shiva y con el sagrado río Ganges. La ciudad ha sido un importante centro de conocimiento, cultura, filosofía, espiritualidad, arte y artesanía durante más de 3.000 años.

Situada cerca de Sarnath, donde Buda pronunció su primer sermón después de alcanzar la iluminación, Varanasi ha desempeñado un papel importante en el desarrollo del hinduismo y el budismo. También es un importante centro de peregrinación jainista y tradicionalmente se considera el lugar de nacimiento de Parsvanath, el vigésimo tercer Tirthankara.

El vaishnavismo y el shaivismo han coexistido durante siglos en Varanasi. La ciudad también está relacionada con el Ayurveda, el sánscrito, el yoga y la literatura hindi. Varanasi es especialmente famosa por su industria de seda y sus brocados de oro y plata.

Varanasi como Centro de Conocimiento y Cultura

Varanasi ha sido un importante centro de educación y actividad intelectual durante siglos. La ciudad está asociada con el sánscrito, la espiritualidad, el misticismo, el yoga y la literatura hindi. Figuras literarias como Premchand y Tulsidas están vinculadas con Varanasi.

La ciudad también ha producido y acogido a reconocidos músicos y artistas. Varanasi es especialmente famosa por sus tradiciones de música clásica, tanto vocal como instrumental, además de la danza tradicional, el teatro, las ferias y los festivales.

Clima de Varanasi

Varanasi tiene un clima cálido y húmedo durante el verano. Las temperaturas pueden alcanzar aproximadamente los 45 °C. El monzón suele llegar a finales de junio o principios de julio y trae fuertes lluvias y una elevada humedad.

Los inviernos son agradables, con temperaturas que pueden descender hasta unos 7 °C. El período más favorable para los turistas suele ser de octubre a abril.

Cómo Llegar a Varanasi

En avión

Varanasi cuenta con el aeropuerto de Babatpur, situado aproximadamente a 22 km de Varanasi y a unos 30 km de Sarnath. La ciudad tiene conexiones aéreas con destinos importantes como Nueva Delhi, Agra, Khajuraho, Kolkata, Mumbai, Lucknow y Bhubaneswar.

En tren

Varanasi es un importante nudo ferroviario y cuenta con trenes que la conectan con las principales ciudades y destinos de la India.

Por carretera

Varanasi está bien conectada por carretera mediante importantes carreteras nacionales. Entre sus principales conexiones se encuentran la NH2 hacia Delhi y Kolkata, la NH7 hacia Kanyakumari y la NH29 hacia Gorakhpur.

Compras en Varanasi

El tejido de seda es una de las industrias tradicionales más famosas de Varanasi. Los saris de seda Banarasi y los brocados ricamente decorados con oro y plata se encuentran entre los productos más populares de la ciudad y tradicionalmente se transmiten de generación en generación.

  • Saris de seda Banarasi
  • Brocados de oro y plata
  • Artículos de latón y cobre
  • Juguetes de madera y arcilla
  • Joyería tradicional
  • Alfombras tejidas a mano
  • Instrumentos musicales
  • Trabajos de zari y artesanía
  • Cuentas de vidrio y brazaletes
  • Estatuas y artículos religiosos

  • Chowk
  • Gyan Vapi

  • Golghar

Cultura de Varanasi

El arte y la cultura de Varanasi están profundamente relacionados con el patrimonio religioso e histórico de la ciudad. La combinación de arqueología, mitología, geografía, arte e historia ha convertido a Varanasi en uno de los principales centros culturales de la India.

La ciudad es famosa por sus textiles tradicionales, artesanías, juguetes, adornos y trabajos en metal, arcilla y madera. Varanasi también ha sido un importante centro educativo, con universidades, colegios, escuelas, madrasas e instituciones tradicionales que mantienen la tradición Guru-Shishya.

La música, el teatro, los festivales y las representaciones tradicionales forman una parte importante de la identidad cultural de Varanasi. La ciudad es especialmente conocida por sus tradiciones de música clásica y por el teatro tradicional como el Ramlila.

content.en:
History of Varanasi

Varanasi, also known as Kashi and Benaras, is one of the oldest living cities in the world and has been an important pilgrimage destination for Hindus for centuries. According to Hindu belief, Varanasi is associated with Lord Shiva and the sacred River Ganges. The city has been a major centre of learning, culture, philosophy, spirituality, arts and crafts for more than 3,000 years.

Located close to Sarnath, where Buddha delivered his first sermon after attaining enlightenment, Varanasi has played an important role in the development of Hinduism and Buddhism. It is also an important pilgrimage centre for Jains and is traditionally believed to be the birthplace of Parshvanath, the twenty-third Tirthankara.

Vaishnavism and Shaivism have coexisted in Varanasi for centuries. The city has also been associated with Ayurveda, Sanskrit, yoga and Hindi literature. Varanasi is particularly famous for its silk and gold and silver brocade industry.

Varanasi as a Centre of Learning and Culture

Varanasi has been an important centre of education and intellectual activity for centuries. The city is associated with Sanskrit, spirituality, mysticism, yoga and Hindi literature. Famous literary figures such as Premchand and Tulsidas are associated with Varanasi.

The city has also produced and welcomed renowned musicians and artists. Varanasi is particularly famous for its classical music traditions, including vocal and instrumental music, as well as traditional dance, theatre, fairs and festivals.

Climate of Varanasi

Varanasi has a hot and humid summer climate. During summer, temperatures can reach around 45°C. The monsoon generally arrives in late June or early July and brings heavy rainfall and high humidity.

Winters are pleasant, with temperatures sometimes falling to around 7°C. The most favourable period for tourists is generally from October to April.

How to Reach Varanasi

By Air

Varanasi is served by the airport at Babatpur, located approximately 22 km from Varanasi and around 30 km from Sarnath. The city has air connections with major destinations including New Delhi, Agra, Khajuraho, Kolkata, Mumbai, Lucknow and Bhubaneswar.

By Train

Varanasi is an important railway junction and is served by trains connecting it with metropolitan cities and major destinations across India.

By Road

Varanasi is well connected by road through major national highways. Important road connections include NH2 towards Delhi and Kolkata, NH7 towards Kanyakumari and NH29 towards Gorakhpur.

Shopping in Varanasi

Silk weaving is one of the most famous traditional industries of Varanasi. Banarasi silk sarees and richly decorated gold and silver brocades are among the city's most popular products and are traditionally passed down through generations.

  • Banarasi silk sarees
  • Gold and silver brocades
  • Brass and copper items
  • Wooden and clay toys
  • Traditional jewellery
  • Handwoven carpets
  • Musical instruments
  • Zari work and handicrafts
  • Glass beads and bangles
  • Religious statues and items

Popular Shopping Areas

  • Chowk
  • Gyan Vapi
  • Vishwanath Gali
  • Thatheri Bazaar
  • Lahurabir
  • Godoulia and Dashashwamedh Gali
  • Golghar

Culture of Varanasi

The art and culture of Varanasi are deeply connected with the city's religious and historical heritage. The combination of archaeology, mythology, geography, art and history has made Varanasi one of India's most important cultural centres.

The city is famous for its traditional textiles, handicrafts, toys, ornaments and metal, clay and woodwork. Varanasi has also remained an important centre of education, with universities, colleges, schools, madrasas and traditional institutions continuing the Guru-Shishya tradition.

Music, theatre, festivals and traditional performances are an important part of Varanasi's cultural identity. The city is particularly renowned for its classical music traditions and traditional theatre such as Ramlila.

content.pt:
História de Vellore

A cidade de Vellore, em Tamil Nadu, deve grande parte de sua importância histórica à construção de seu forte no século XIV d.C., destinado a proteger a cidade durante as Guerras Carnáticas. O Templo Jalakanteshwarar e o Lago Elagiri também contribuíram para aumentar o interesse turístico por Vellore.

Vellore está localizada às margens do rio Palar, a uma altitude superior a 200 metros acima do nível do mar. A cidade possui um clima moderado, com brisas marítimas provenientes da Baía de Bengala durante grande parte do ano.

Hotéis em Vellore

A maioria dos hotéis de Vellore está convenientemente localizada no centro comercial da cidade e em seus arredores. Vellore fica a aproximadamente 140 quilômetros de Chennai, capital de Tamil Nadu, oferecendo fácil acesso ao Aeroporto Internacional de Chennai.

Os hotéis de Vellore oferecem quartos confortáveis equipados com as comodidades necessárias para os viajantes. Seus restaurantes servem culinária indiana, chinesa e continental, incluindo opções vegetarianas e não vegetarianas.

Para viajantes a negócios, vários hotéis oferecem salas de conferências e espaços para banquetes, equipados com serviços como telefone STD/ISD, Internet e serviços de secretaria. Alguns hotéis também possuem academias e salões.

Como Chegar a Vellore

De avião

O aeroporto principal mais próximo de Vellore é o Aeroporto Internacional de Chennai. Chennai possui boas conexões aéreas com as principais cidades da Índia e outros destinos. De Chennai, é possível continuar a viagem até Vellore de ônibus ou trem.

De trem

A estação ferroviária mais próxima é Katpadi, localizada a cerca de 6 quilômetros de Vellore. Katpadi fica na linha ferroviária Chennai-Bangalore-Mumbai e possui boas conexões com Tamil Nadu e outras regiões da Índia. Há trens expressos e super-rápidos para vários destinos.

Por estrada

Vellore está localizada na importante rodovia Chennai-Bangalore. A cidade possui boas conexões com outras partes do sul da Índia por meio de uma rede de rodovias estaduais e nacionais.

A Corporação de Transporte de Tamil Nadu e operadores privados oferecem serviços de ônibus entre Vellore e várias cidades de Tamil Nadu e regiões próximas.

content.en:
History of Vellore

Vellore, in Tamil Nadu, owes much of its historical importance to the construction of its fort in the 14th century AD, which was built to protect the city during the Carnatic Wars. The Jalakanteshwarar Temple and Elagiri Lake have also added to Vellore's appeal among visitors.

Vellore is situated on the banks of the Palar River at an altitude of more than 200 metres above sea level. The city enjoys a moderate climate, with sea breezes from the Bay of Bengal blowing for much of the year.

Hotels in Vellore

Most hotels in Vellore are conveniently located in and around the city's commercial centre. Vellore is approximately 140 kilometres from Chennai, the capital of Tamil Nadu, and provides convenient access to Chennai International Airport.

Hotels in Vellore offer comfortable rooms equipped with the amenities expected by travellers. Their restaurants serve Indian, Chinese and Continental cuisine, including both vegetarian and non-vegetarian options.

For business travellers, several hotels provide conference rooms and banquet facilities equipped with services such as STD/ISD telephone facilities, Internet and secretarial services. Some hotels also offer gyms and lounges.

How to Reach Vellore

By Air

The nearest major airport to Vellore is Chennai International Airport. Chennai is well connected to major cities in India and other destinations by air. From Chennai, travellers can continue to Vellore by bus or train.

By Train

The nearest railway station is Katpadi, located about 6 kilometres from Vellore. Katpadi lies on the Chennai-Bangalore-Mumbai railway line and is well connected with Tamil Nadu and other parts of India. Express and super-fast trains are available to several destinations.

By Road

Vellore lies on the busy Chennai-Bangalore highway. The city is well connected with other parts of southern India through a network of state and national highways.

Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporation and private operators provide bus services between Vellore and neighbouring cities in Tamil Nadu and surrounding areas.

content.es:
Viaje a Yanam

Historia de Yanam

Yanam es una de las regiones de Pondicherry y se encuentra en la costa oriental de la India. La región está situada donde los ríos Koringa y Gautami se separan y está rodeada por el río Godavari Gowthami hacia el este y el sur.

Yanam tiene una historia de aproximadamente 300 años vinculada a la presencia francesa. Aunque geográficamente se encuentra en Andhra Pradesh, políticamente forma parte de Pondicherry, lo que le otorga una identidad cultural y administrativa particular.

Geografía y agricultura de Yanam

La región de Yanam es principalmente llana y posee suelos aluviales adecuados para diferentes tipos de cultivos.

  • Arroz
  • Tabaco
  • Coco
  • Jowar
  • Ragi
  • Legumbres
  • Cilantro
  • Fenogreco

Pesca en Yanam

La pesca es una actividad importante en la región. Entre las principales zonas pesqueras se encuentran Gulrimpeta, Agraharam, Kothapeta, Mettakur, Kanakalapeta, Kursampeta, Padvarevupeta y Sangadirerupeta.

El dhony, una especie de canoa, es una de las embarcaciones pesqueras más utilizadas. También se utiliza otro tipo de embarcación conocida como Padona. Las capturas incluyen salmonetes, hilsa, gambas, bagres y otras especies.

Cómo llegar a Yanam

Por carretera

Yanam está conectada por carretera con importantes ciudades cercanas de Andhra Pradesh, como Kakinada, Rajahmundry y Visakhapatnam. También existen conexiones por carretera con otras ciudades de la región.

Por tren

La estación de tren más cercana se encuentra en Kakinada, a unos 26 km de Yanam. Kakinada cuenta con conexiones ferroviarias hacia Chennai y otros destinos importantes.

Templo Venkanna Babu

El templo Venkanna Babu también es conocido como Chaldikudu Venkanna Temple y Meesala Venkanna Temple. Según la información proporcionada, el templo fue construido por los reyes de Rajamahendravaram, actualmente conocida como Rajahmundry, durante el siglo XV.

El templo es conocido por la imagen de la deidad, que presenta grandes bigotes, característica que recuerda al Señor Sathyanarayana Swamy de Annavaram.

Festival Venkanna

El Festival Venkanna se celebra cada año durante el mes de marzo y continúa durante aproximadamente un mes. El Kalyanam del Señor Venkateswara es uno de los acontecimientos principales.

  • Ponnavahanam
  • Radha Yatra
  • Chakrateertham
  • Kalyanam del Señor Venkateswara

Durante estos días, numerosos devotos visitan Yanam para participar en las celebraciones y buscar las bendiciones del Señor Venkanna Babu.

Venkanna Ratham

El Venkanna Ratham es un carro ceremonial que pesa aproximadamente 15 toneladas. Fue construido en 1950 y posteriormente renovado después de sufrir daños durante un fuerte ciclón en 1996.

El Ratham se transporta durante las celebraciones por una parte de Yanam y es acompañado por devotos que participan con cánticos y bhajans.

La Gran Mezquita de Yanam

El terreno para la mezquita fue donado por el Gobierno francés en 1848. Inicialmente se construyó una pequeña mezquita, que posteriormente fue remodelada y sustituida por una nueva construcción.

La mezquita fue ampliada durante el período 1999-2000 y actualmente puede acoger aproximadamente a 200 personas para las oraciones.

  • Ramzan
  • Bakrid
  • Milad Nabi

Estas celebraciones se realizan con especial importancia cada año. La mezquita también atiende a comunidades de localidades cercanas de Andhra Pradesh.

Iglesia Católica de Yanam

La iglesia católica es uno de los recuerdos de la presencia francesa en Yanam. Fue construida en estilo europeo y sus muebles y elementos decorativos fueron importados de Francia.

La construcción comenzó en el siglo XIX y fue completada en 1846. El edificio conserva elementos relacionados con la historia de los gobernantes y misioneros franceses de la región.

Festival de María Maa

Según la historia local proporcionada, cada año en marzo se celebra un festival dedicado a María Maa. Devotos de diferentes lugares cercanos visitan el lugar para participar en las celebraciones.

Una característica destacada del festival es la participación de personas pertenecientes a diferentes comunidades religiosas, incluidos cristianos, musulmanes e hindúes.

content.en:
Travel to Yanam

History of Yanam

Yanam is one of the regions of Pondicherry and is located on the eastern coast of India. The region lies where the Koringa and Gautami rivers separate and is surrounded by the Godavari Gowthami River towards the east and south.

Yanam has a history of around 300 years associated with French rule. Although geographically located in Andhra Pradesh, it is politically part of Pondicherry, giving the region a distinctive cultural and administrative identity.

Geography and Agriculture of Yanam

Yanam is largely a flat region with alluvial soil suitable for several agricultural crops.

  • Rice
  • Tobacco
  • Coconut
  • Jowar
  • Ragi
  • Pulses
  • Coriander
  • Fenugreek

Fishing in Yanam

Fishing is an important activity in the region. Major fishing areas include Gulrimpeta, Agraharam, Kothapeta, Mettakur, Kanakalapeta, Kursampeta, Padvarevupeta and Sangadirerupeta.

The dhony, a type of canoe, is one of the commonly used fishing boats. Another type of boat known as Padona is also used. The catch includes mullet, hilsa, prawns, catfish and other species.

How to Reach Yanam

By Road

Yanam is connected by road with important nearby cities of Andhra Pradesh, including Kakinada, Rajahmundry and Visakhapatnam.

By Train

The nearest railway station is located at Kakinada, approximately 26 km from Yanam. Kakinada is connected by rail with Chennai and other important destinations.

Venkanna Babu Temple

The Venkanna Babu Temple is also known as Chaldikudu Venkanna Temple and Meesala Venkanna Temple. According to the provided information, the temple was built by the rulers of Rajamahendravaram, now known as Rajahmundry, during the 15th century.

The temple is known for the deity's image featuring large moustaches, a distinctive feature associated with Lord Sathyanarayana Swamy of Annavaram.

Venkanna Festival

The Venkanna Festival is celebrated every year in March and continues for approximately one month. The Kalyanam of Lord Venkateswara is one of the main events.

  • Ponnavahanam
  • Radha Yatra
  • Chakrateertham
  • Lord Venkateswara Kalyanam

During the festival, numerous devotees visit Yanam to participate in the celebrations and seek the blessings of Lord Venkanna Babu.

Venkanna Ratham

The Venkanna Ratham is a ceremonial chariot weighing approximately 15 tonnes. It was built in 1950 and later renovated after being partially damaged by a severe cyclone in 1996.

The Ratham is taken through part of Yanam during the celebrations and is accompanied by devotees chanting prayers and performing bhajans.

The Grand Mosque of Yanam

The site for the mosque was donated by the French Government in 1848. A small mosque was initially built and was later renovated and replaced by a new structure.

The mosque was expanded during 1999-2000 and can accommodate approximately 200 people for prayers.

  • Ramzan
  • Bakrid
  • Milad Nabi

These occasions are celebrated with great importance every year. The mosque also serves communities from nearby villages in Andhra Pradesh.

Catholic Church of Yanam

The Catholic Church is one of the reminders of the French presence in Yanam. It was built in a European architectural style, with furniture and decorative elements imported from France.

The church was completed in 1846 and preserves elements associated with the history of French rulers and missionaries in the region.

Maria Maa Festival

According to the local history provided, an important festival dedicated to Maria Maa is celebrated every year in March. Devotees from different nearby areas visit the site to participate in the celebrations.

A notable feature of the festival is the participation of people from different religious communities, including Christians, Muslims and Hindus.
